source.title: Turning the Spell Around: Lightweight Alignment Amplification via Rank-One Safety Injection
source.authors: H. Shairah; Hasan Abed Al Kader Hammoud; G. Turkiyyah; Bernard Ghanem

record.tranche_reason: Tests a difference-in-means safety direction by applying it through a rank-one weight edit and measuring refusal and utility. It does not reproduce the original activation projection or ablation.
record.gate_note: The paper measures ROSI outcomes, not the values used to select the layer or direction. The original-method activation ablation and direct activation addition are not performed. The paper also evaluates jailbreak benchmarks, but those results do not test whether attacks suppress the direction. For the transfer table, the printed numeric layout is difficult to assign confidently; transfer rows below rely on the authors’ explicit prose rather than unassigned table numbers.
record.test_reason: ROSI adds the harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction to all residual-stream write matrices as a rank-one weight edit. It then measures harmful refusal, benign compliance and utility. This tests the 'adding the direction induces refusal, abilities kept' part of V1 with a different method. Appendix B tests cross-lingual and cross-model (Qwen 14B↔32B) transfer of the direction, which bears on V6. No ablation or removal of refusal is run.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that ROSI raises refusal and jailbreak robustness in aligned models and re-aligns uncensored models with negligible utility loss, and that uncensored models need a safety system prompt to extract a usable direction. In appendices they add three findings. Injecting before fine-tuning preserves safety while post-hoc repair barely helps. Vectors transfer across English/Arabic and between Qwen 14B/32B. One sample pair suffices for extraction.
record.recipe_differences: Uses harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means at a selected layer and prompt-token position, then performs a permanent rank-one weight update to residual-stream write matrices. It does not project the direction out of activations at every layer and position, nor directly add the vector to activations.
record.method_sensitivity: The selected layer is chosen using validation prompts. For uncensored models, a safety system prompt during extraction substantially changes the outcome. English/Arabic transfer strength varies by model and evaluation language; cross-model vector performance also varies.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding the refusal direction by weight edit lowers jailbreak attack success rates across DAN, HarmBench, WildGuardTest and WildJailbreak (Tables 2, 5, 9).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Amplifying the diff-in-means refusal direction increases robustness to jailbreaks.

fits_no_version.finding: In Dolphin-Qwen-3B, a safety system prompt increases PCA separation of harmful and harmless activations (centroid distance 34.4→40.1). This is a representational measure, not refusal behaviour.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Uncensoring fine-tuning blurs harmful/harmless separation, which prompting can restore.

record.problems: No uncertainty is given for the tabulated refusal and utility scores. Cross-lingual Table 8’s flattened numeric layout does not support confident assignment of all values. Several aligned models have near-ceiling baseline refusal, limiting measurable gains. ROSI is not a standalone jailbreak defense, as the authors acknowledge.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 and Table 5 jailbreak benchmark results are not included because they report ROSI performance but do not test whether attacks suppress the refusal direction (V3). Most per-benchmark utility results in Tables 3 and 6 are omitted; selected notable declines and the paper’s aggregate utility statements are retained. Table 9’s non-DAN attack metrics are omitted to stay within 60 rows. Appendix C extraction-set-size results and Figure 2 layer-selection ablations do not directly measure the named versions’ claimed refusal mechanism or transfer.

untested.parts: Ablating the direction to remove refusal. Direct activation addition. Whether adding the direction induces refusal on harmless prompts (ROSI uses a small push, and BC is measured only as a side effect).
Transfer from base to instruct models. Transfer across architectures beyond one same-family size pair.
Not tested; jailbreak ASR is reported, but suppression of the direction by attacks is not.
Not tested; higher-rank updates are explicitly left unexplored.
Not tested directly (see notes on Dolphin).

missing.what: Injecting only at the source layer gives modest HR gains. HR stabilises once about 30–40% of layers are injected, and varies with which random layers are chosen. This makes the V1 effect depend on the layer choice.
A direction from a single harmful/harmless pair raises Qwen-3B HR from 89.8 to 99.1; the authors read this as a dominant direction.
Cross-lingual numeric values (now given in row_fixes). Also the same-language Arabic result for Yi: the Arabic vector on Arabic prompts reaches only 50.9, from a 34.6 baseline.
Cross-model utility is stable (BoolQ about −2 for 14B either vector; others within ±1).

record.verdict_notes: The study only adds the direction; it never ablates it. The Dolphin no-prompt results (direction ineffective or harmful in 3 of 4 uncensored models) loosely suggest that uncensoring fine-tuning can erase an extractable refusal direction, which is relevant to V7. However, the study does not frame or test this as V7, so no V7 verdict is given. The record's limits_scope for Yi transfer is not supported by Table 8 and was replaced. No uncertainty is reported for any table value.

versions.untested_parts: Does not ablate the direction at every layer and position or directly add it to activations. Benign compliance is measured, but the paper does not separately report a direct false-refusal rate on harmless prompts.
No weight edit that removes refusal or abliteration is evaluated.
Jailbreak success is measured after ROSI, but attacks are not tested for suppressing the direction, and training against ablation is not evaluated.
No comparison of one direction against an affine subspace, cone, or multiple directions.
No separate measurement of harmfulness judgment and refusal decision.
Tests English/Arabic transfer and transfer between two Qwen variants with shared hidden size; it does not test transfer from base to instruct models.
Tests the order of ROSI and fine-tuning for refusal retention, but not whether training determines the existence of a removable refusal direction.

tranche.reason: ROSI adds the harmful-minus-harmless diff-in-means direction to the weights, a different method from activation addition and ablation. It reports refusal rates (HR/BC) and capability. Appendix B asks directly whether the direction is language- or model-specific. It is a method paper, so it is borderline T4, but its measured outcome is the effect of adding the direction itself.

source_check.notes: Table 8's lost layout is confirmed by matching Table 1: Base-En is 79.5/95.8/81.3 and ROSI-En/En is 92.7/100/99.5. Rows r39-r44 still hold prose placeholders and must be filled from Table 8. The authors call Yi's Arabic transfer 'weaker', yet their own table shows the English vector beating the Arabic-own vector on Arabic (77.8 vs 50.9). The study has no random-direction control and no CIs on Tables 8-9, and its Arabic prompts are Gemma-3-27B translations. The text cites Table 3 for cross-model utility; it likely means Table 10.

statements.correction: ROSI: diff-in-means extracted at one selected layer; rank-one update W_out + alpha*s*w_bar^T applied to every residual-stream write matrix. Arabic extraction and test prompts were translated from English by Gemma-3-27B. HR is judged on CatQA by Llama Guard 3. Table 8 reports no CIs or n beyond the 550 CatQA prompts.
statements.problem: The numbers for this study are right (r40 79.5->92.0, r44 81.3->100.0, r43 34.6->77.8, r41 98.0->100.0). But the conditions say ROSI's direction is 'applied at a selected layer'. ROSI only extracts at a selected layer and injects into all residual-stream write matrices. The 'uncertainty' in 'why' does not cover Table 8: the only CIs are for the Fig. 2b layer ablation.

Minor: the generic condition 'addition or steering at a selected layer' does not fit ROSI, which is a rank-one edit to all residual-stream write matrices. The claim about this study is right: DAN 32.3->5.0, equal to 14B's own vector (5.0) and better than it on the other five Table 9 metrics.

statements.correction: Qwen2.5-14B vector on Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct: DAN 42.0->28.7, WG-Micro 18.4->12.5, WG-Adv 14.8->11.9, WG-Vanilla 28.2->22.9, HarmBench 3.9->2.9, WildJailbreak 83.3->76.9. All are improvements, each smaller than with 32B's own vector. The authors say both directions give 'meaningful gains'.
statements.problem: The numbers are right (DAN 42.0->28.7, -13.3 vs -20.3 native). But they are cited under a 'challenges' entry. In this study the 14B->32B transfer does not fail: it gives gains on all six Table 9 metrics, only smaller than the native vector's. That is limits_scope (the record's own verdict). The reverse transfer (32B->14B) matches or beats native.
